# Validate tool input against the registered inputSchema

Issue: re-cinq/HALEngine#37
Labels: priority:medium, type:feature, size:M, area:tools, epic:extension-points

Part of #35

## Why

`ToolRegistry.execute` looks a tool up, logs the input's key names, and calls the executor
without ever checking the declared `inputSchema` (`src/orchestration/tools/registry.ts`).
Every tool declares a JSON Schema (`src/types/ai.ts`) that is handed verbatim to both
providers, but nothing validates what comes back from the model. The shipped example shows the
shape of the problem: `example/weather-tool.ts` declares `location` as a required string, then
casts and defaults it (`(input.location as string) || 'Unknown'`) with a comment warning the reader
that `inputSchema` shapes what the model sends but does not enforce it. That is the careful version,
written by the people who wrote the engine — and it still answers a malformed call with a
confidently formatted forecast for `'Unknown'` rather than telling the model it got the call wrong.

The registry currently pushes this check onto each tool's own executor, leaving every consumer
to implement it itself — differently each time, or not at all. A tool that receives unexpected input must fail
in one predictable, known way before the rest of this epic's tool work can be built on top
of it.

## What to do

Validate `input` against the resolved tool definition's `inputSchema` inside
`ToolRegistry.execute`, before the executor runs, using a JSON Schema validator (`ajv`
unless the build proves otherwise) added to `dependencies` — not a second, hand-written
schema in a different format, since the schema already has to match what is handed to the
providers.

Compile a static tool's schema once at `register` time so a broken schema fails at startup,
not mid-conversation; a schema produced by a function-valued `ToolDefinitionSource`
resolves and compiles per call, cached by the resolved schema object.

A rejection returns a `ToolResponse` (`{result: '<what was wrong>'}`) rather than throwing,
so a malformed call becomes something the model can read and correct within the existing
`DEFAULT_MAX_TOOL_ROUNDS = 5` budget, instead of ending the whole conversation with a
generic transport error. Validation enforces `required`, declared types and `enum` only —
it does not inject `additionalProperties: false`, coerce types, or apply defaults, and
there is no opt-out flag.

Update `docs/adding-a-tool.md`, `README.md` and `.specify/spec.md` to match.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `ToolRegistry.execute` validates `input` against the resolved definition's
      `inputSchema` before calling the executor; on failure it returns a `ToolResponse`
      whose `result` describes the failure, and the executor is never invoked
- [ ] A new `src/orchestration/tools/registry.test.ts` (the registry has no test file today)
      registers a tool requiring a `location` string, calls `execute` with `{}`, and
      asserts the returned result names `location` as required and the executor's call
      count is `0`
- [ ] A test asserts valid input with an unlisted extra property is passed through to the
      executor unchanged (`toEqual`, so an added default or coerced value fails the test) —
      exactly once
- [ ] A test asserts a wrong-typed field (a number where a string is required) is rejected
      with a message naming the field path and the expected type, and that the message does
      **not** contain the offending value
- [ ] A test asserts `register` throws at registration time for an uncompilable schema, and
      that the thrown message names the tool
- [ ] A test asserts a function-valued tool definition whose returned schema differs between
      calls is validated against the schema current at that call, not a stale cached one
- [ ] A test asserts a static tool's schema is compiled once across ten `execute` calls
- [ ] A tool-loop test in `chatOrchestrator.test.ts` drives a stub provider through a
      rejected tool call followed by a corrected retry, and asserts `processMessage`
      resolves — not rejects — with the rejection text visible to the provider on the next
      round
- [ ] `execute` still throws `Unknown tool: <name>` for an unregistered name, unchanged,
      pinned by a test
- [ ] Rejection messages and log lines name the failing property paths and the constraint
      that failed, and never a property **value**. Tool input is where identifying data
      enters the engine and the engine redacts nothing today. A test asserts a rejected
      payload containing an identifying field produces no log line and no returned text
      containing that field's value
- [ ] `execute` carries a **one-line** doc comment — `re-lint/max-comment-lines` rejects a
      `@param`/`@returns`/`@throws` block — and the full contract (rejection `ToolResponse` for input
      the schema rejects, throw only for an unknown tool name) is stated in
      `specs/hal-engine-tool-input-validation/spec.md`, which the comment points at
- [ ] The validator is in `package.json` `dependencies`, not `peerDependencies` or
      `devDependencies`, and
      `npm run build && node --input-type=module -e "import('./dist/index.js')"` exits `0`
- [ ] `README.md` states what the registry now does, and the claim is true rather than
      merely present
- [ ] `docs/adding-a-tool.md` no longer tells executors to cast defensively and handle
      missing input; it states that input reaching an executor has already passed the
      declared schema, that unknown keys may still be present, and that a rejection is
      returned to the model rather than thrown
- [ ] `.specify/spec.md` records that a rejection is a tool result (not an exception), that
      the tool-round bound is what stops a retry cycle from spinning, and that extra
      properties pass through unmodified
- [ ] The PR body states the migration note: an executor that used to hand-validate its
      input now receives only input the schema already accepts, and a tool that relied on
      seeing malformed input to produce its own error message stops seeing it. The version
      bump is MINOR
- [ ] Every test this issue adds cites the statement it validates with an inline
      `([validated by ...])` link in a `specs/**` or `adrs/**` file, and the statements exist
      before the tests do. `re-lint/require-spec-link` fails the build on an uncited test, so the
      spec edits are part of this issue rather than a follow-up
- [ ] `CHANGELOG.md` carries an entry for this change, written for somebody reading it on npm
      rather than somebody reading this repo's log. CI runs `scripts/check-changelog.sh` and
      fails any PR touching a non-test file under `src/` without one
- [ ] `npm run build`, `npm run typecheck`, `npm test`, `npm run eslint` (`--max-warnings 0`)
      and `npm run prettier:check` pass, with no `any` in the changed public surface

## Tech notes

Today's `throw` in `registry.ts` propagates through the orchestrator's tool-call
`Promise.all`, out of the processing loop's `try`, fires `onError`, and reaches the
WebSocket error handler, which sends a generic "Failed to process message" and never sends
the stream-end frame. That end-to-end path is why a rejection has to be a returned
`ToolResponse` instead of a throw.

Deliberately out of scope: the `Unknown tool: <name>` throw stays as-is — the same failure
class handled the opposite way, which is an intentional split, but changing it affects
direct callers and is tracked as *Return an unknown tool name to the model instead of
throwing*. Also out of scope: validating tool *output*; hallucination detection and an
evaluation harness; per-tool authorization — a schema-valid call for someone else's data is still
valid, and authorization is a separate `ToolContext` boundary concern that no issue in this epic
owns (*Let a consumer decline a tool call through a `beforeToolCall` hook* is a veto seam, not an
authorization model); retry, timeout
and rate limiting around tool execution; and any actual tool implementation, which is
written against this contract later.

# Definition of Done

> `ToolRegistry.execute` looks a tool up, logs the input's key names, and calls the executor
> without ever checking the declared `inputSchema` (`src/orchestration/tools/registry.ts`).
> Every tool declares a JSON Schema (`src/types/ai.ts`) that is handed verbatim to both
> providers, but nothing validates what comes back from the model.

**Strategy: `direct`** — `ToolRegistry.register`, `ToolRegistry.execute` and `createChatOrchestrator` already expose the exact entry points this ticket changes, so the acceptance tests call them directly today and fail because schema compilation and input validation are absent.

## Done when these pass

- [ ] **rejects input missing a required property with a ToolResponse and never calls the executor** — `ToolRegistry.execute` validates `input` against `inputSchema`, returns a `ToolResponse` naming the missing required property, and does not invoke the executor.
  `src/orchestration/tools/registry.acceptance.test.ts`

- [ ] **rejects a wrong-typed property naming the field and expected type without leaking the offending value to the result or logs** — `ToolRegistry.execute` rejects a property with the wrong JSON Schema type without calling the executor, names the failing field path and expected type in `result`, and omits the offending property value from both `result` and emitted log lines.
  `src/orchestration/tools/registry.acceptance.test.ts`

- [ ] **throws at register time naming the tool when a static inputSchema cannot be compiled** — `ToolRegistry.register` compiles a static `ToolDefinition`'s `inputSchema` once at registration time and throws synchronously naming the tool when the schema is invalid.
  `src/orchestration/tools/registry.acceptance.test.ts`

- [ ] **returns a schema rejection as a tool_result in the orchestrator loop so the model can correct the call on the next round** — `createChatOrchestrator` feeds a schema-rejected tool call's `ToolResponse.result` back to the provider as a `tool_result` without invoking the executor on the invalid call, allowing the model to retry with valid arguments and complete the turn.
  `src/orchestration/tools/registry.acceptance.test.ts`

## Facets

- [x] Add `ajv` to `dependencies` in `package.json` and `package-lock.json` (`strict: false`, `validateFormats: false`, no coercion, no defaults, no injected `additionalProperties: false`) and bump the package version `MINOR`.
- [ ] Compile static `ToolDefinition.inputSchema` at `ToolRegistry.register` time (throwing an error naming the tool on invalid schemas) and cache compiled validators for function-valued `ToolDefinitionSource` schemas by schema object reference (`WeakMap`).
- [x] Validate `input` in `ToolRegistry.execute` before invoking the executor, returning a `ToolResponse` (`{result}`) that names failing field paths and expected types/required fields without echoing or logging offending values, and add the one-line doc comment pointing at `specs/hal-engine-tool-input-validation/spec.md`.
- [ ] Add unit tests in `src/orchestration/tools/registry.test.ts` and `src/orchestration/chatOrchestrator.test.ts`, link the remaining statements in `specs/hal-engine-tool-input-validation/spec.md`, and update `example/weather-tool.ts`, `docs/adding-a-tool.md`, `README.md`, `.specify/spec.md`, `adrs/ADR-002-response-validation.md`, and `CHANGELOG.md`.

## Out of scope

- Output validation and domain sanity checks (covered by ADR-002), MCP tool-server discovery and proxying (#42), per-tool authorization or `beforeToolCall` hooks (#40), retry/timeout/rate-limiting around tool execution, and concrete tool implementations.

README.md:10:- **Tool system**: Register custom tools with a JSON Schema `inputSchema`, executed in parallel within a configurable tool loop. The registry validates each call before the executor runs; rejected input is returned to the model as a tool result, while unknown tool names still throw
README.md:23:That is the supported install path, and the one this project releases against: every published version is built by a workflow run in this repository's CI and carries an npm provenance attestation. `npm audit signatures` verifies it, which tells you the tarball was built by a workflow of this repository from the commit the attestation names, rather than uploaded by whoever held a token. `0.2.0` was published once with a token, because the registry cannot hold a trusted publisher for a name that has never been published; every version after it is published by the release workflow from a published GitHub release, with no credential stored anywhere, and reaches you only after a maintainer approves it.
README.md:27:That last one has a trap in it. An existing `"hal-engine": "github:…"` entry keeps resolving after the rename — the directory is still `node_modules/hal-engine`, so `import 'hal-engine'` keeps working while the package inside it declares `@re-cinq/hal-engine`. The rename produces no error, no warning and no failed build. Worse, following the rename and switching your imports to `@re-cinq/hal-engine` is what breaks: that specifier resolves to nothing until the key is renamed too. Move to the registry specifier, or rename the key and the imports together.

specs/hal-engine-tool-input-validation/spec.md:8:Every tool registered in `src/orchestration/tools/registry.ts` declares a JSON Schema `inputSchema` that is forwarded to the configured AI provider, and `ToolRegistry.execute` validates the model-supplied `input` against that schema before calling the tool's executor. When validation fails, `execute` returns a rejection `ToolResponse` describing what was wrong rather than throwing, so the orchestrator feeds the failure back to the model as a `tool_result` within the existing tool-round budget.
specs/hal-engine-tool-input-validation/spec.md:12:- When `input` omits a property listed in `required`, `ToolRegistry.execute` returns a `ToolResponse` whose `result` names the missing property path as required and never invokes the executor ([validated by: returns a required-property rejection without invoking the executor](../../src/orchestration/tools/registry.test.ts#L5), [nested path](../../src/orchestration/tools/registry.test.ts#L27)).
specs/hal-engine-tool-input-validation/spec.md:13:- When `input` supplies a property whose value does not match its declared JSON Schema type, `ToolRegistry.execute` returns a `ToolResponse` naming the failing field path and expected type without invoking the executor, and neither `result` nor the emitted log record contains the offending property value ([validated by: rejects a wrong-typed property naming the field and expected type without leaking the offending value to the result or logs](../../src/orchestration/tools/registry.acceptance.test.ts#L48)).
specs/hal-engine-tool-input-validation/spec.md:14:- When `input` satisfies `required`, declared property types and `enum`, `ToolRegistry.execute` invokes the executor once and passes the input object through unchanged — including undeclared extra properties — without injecting `additionalProperties: false`, coercing types or applying defaults.
specs/hal-engine-tool-input-validation/spec.md:15:- When `ToolRegistry.execute` is called with a tool name that has not been registered, it throws `Unknown tool: <name>` because an unregistered tool is a programming or configuration error rather than a recoverable input mistake.
specs/hal-engine-tool-input-validation/spec.md:19:- A static `ToolDefinition` has its `inputSchema` compiled once at `register` time, so a schema that is not valid JSON Schema throws synchronously from `register` with an error message naming the offending tool ([validated by: throws at register time naming the tool when a static inputSchema cannot be compiled](../../src/orchestration/tools/registry.acceptance.test.ts#L97)).
specs/hal-engine-tool-input-validation/spec.md:20:- A static tool's `inputSchema` is compiled at `register` time and reused on every `execute` call without re-reading or re-compiling `definition.inputSchema` ([validated by: reuses a static schema validator across ten executions](../../src/orchestration/tools/registry.test.ts#L50)).
specs/hal-engine-tool-input-validation/spec.md:21:- A function-valued `ToolDefinitionSource` resolves its definition on each `execute` call and validates against the `inputSchema` returned for that call, caching compiled validators by schema object reference (`WeakMap`) so distinct returned schemas each enforce their own rules.
specs/hal-engine-tool-input-validation/spec.md:25:- Because a schema rejection returns a `ToolResponse` instead of throwing, `src/orchestration/chatOrchestrator.ts` sends the rejection `result` back to the provider as a `tool_result` message, allowing the model to issue a corrected tool call on the next round and complete the turn within `maxToolRounds` ([validated by: returns a schema rejection as a tool_result in the orchestrator loop so the model can correct the call on the next round](../../src/orchestration/tools/registry.acceptance.test.ts#L116)).

specs/hal-engine-npm-release/spec.md:8:This package has never been published. It is `hal-engine@0.1.0`, CommonJS, unlicensed, and reachable only through a git specifier that clones the repository and builds from source. This spec describes what has to become true for `npm install @re-cinq/hal-engine` to resolve from the public registry: the module format it ships, the manifest that describes it, the pipeline that releases it from a published GitHub release without a stored token, and the handful of defects a first public release must not carry — an authentication fallback that opens a chat API, a hook that is declared and never called, a factory arm that drops its configuration, and an optional peer that is not optional. It also covers the documentation, because npm renders `README.md` and nothing else.
specs/hal-engine-npm-release/spec.md:118:The gate runs immediately before `npm publish`, so the two ways it can report a clean tree without having checked one are part of its contract rather than details of its implementation. It shells out to `npm audit`, whose registry failures are themselves JSON and carry no `vulnerabilities` key; and an acceptance names an advisory, which means an acceptance recorded for one advisory must not absorb the next one in the same package.
specs/hal-engine-npm-release/spec.md:120:- A report carrying no vulnerability data fails the check rather than reading as nothing-to-report ([validated by: refuses to report clean when npm returns its registry-failure document](../../scripts/check-audit.test.ts#L81)).
specs/hal-engine-npm-release/spec.md:197:- The version is staged rather than published outright. `npm stage publish` puts the tarball, its dist-tag and its provenance on the registry and leaves the version uninstallable until a maintainer approves it with 2FA, on the package page or through `npm stage approve`. The tag still triggers everything and CI still builds what ships; what changes is that the one irreversible step waits on a human holding a second factor, so a tag pushed by mistake costs an approval nobody gives rather than a version nobody can replace. It also puts proof-of-presence back into a flow that removed it - tokenless publishing has no human in it by design, which is the point of it and also its whole risk.
specs/hal-engine-npm-release/spec.md:213:The same guard holds `CHANGELOG.md` to the version being tagged. `check-changelog.sh` asks only that the file was touched, so the release rename was ungated, and the version reached the registry under a heading that never named it.
specs/hal-engine-npm-release/spec.md:240:- It publishes rather than stages, which is the one place the bootstrap cannot follow the release path. `npm stage publish` answers `404 Package "@re-cinq/hal-engine" not found` against a name the registry has never seen: a stage is approved from the package's Versions tab, so there has to be a package. It was measured rather than assumed - the same workflow on the same commit moved from `403 Unauthorized` to that 404 when the token was corrected, which locates the refusal in the lookup rather than in the credential. So `0.2.0` is the only version that reaches the registry without an approval, and dispatching the workflow is that approval.
specs/hal-engine-npm-release/spec.md:365:- No deprecation window was needed. This package has never been published, so there were no registry consumers to deprecate for, and the window would only ever have been cheap before the first release.
specs/hal-engine-npm-release/spec.md:399:- A `SECURITY.md` states the intake channel, the acknowledgement target, the supported versions, a coordinated-disclosure statement, and an explicit in-scope list naming at minimum the transport layer, the tool registry and the provider adapters.
specs/hal-engine-npm-release/spec.md:401:- `package.json` carries the address in `bugs`, so it survives into registry metadata.
specs/hal-engine-npm-release/spec.md:415:- An Install section above the quick start names the registry specifier as the supported path, and states what the git specifier does differently: it builds `dist` from a checkout via `prepare`, carries no provenance attestation, holds whatever commit the lockfile pinned, and installs under the dependency's key rather than its name — so the existing `"hal-engine": "github:…"` entry keeps resolving silently after the rename, with no failure mode to surface it. Measured, not reasoned: installing the packed tarball under the key `hal-engine` puts a package declaring `@re-cinq/hal-engine` at `node_modules/hal-engine`, where `import 'hal-engine'` loads it and `import '@re-cinq/hal-engine'` fails with `ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND`. Following the rename is what breaks, not ignoring it.
